matched_queries: UK employment guidance: Eligibility and qualifying service for paternity leave and unpaid parental leave, including entitlement from starting employment.
Discover UK employment guidance for Paternity leave: entitlement. Task relevance is separate from current law, commencement and a need to edit.

passages.quote:
Earnings affected by a backdated pay rise

If your employee is entitled to Statutory Neonatal Care Pay, and gets a backdated pay rise that increases the amount of gross earnings already paid in the relevant period, you must:

use the new gross earnings to work their new average weekly earnings

pay any extra Statutory Neonatal Care Pay due

If they were not entitled to Statutory Neonatal Care Pay, and they get a backdated pay rise in the relevant period, you must:

use their new gross earnings to work out their new average weekly earnings

check if they’re eligible for Statutory Neonatal Care Pay

pay any Statutory Neonatal Care Pay due

Underpayments or overpayments of earnings

If underpayments or overpayments of earnings affect your existing employee’s average weekly earnings, they will also affect their entitlement of Statutory Neonatal Care Pay.

If your employee has been:

overpaid, they may have received too much Statutory Neonatal Care Pay (and will have to pay it back through payroll)

underpaid, they have not received the correct Statutory Neonatal Care Pay

If your employee is new, and there are underpayments or overpayments of earnings that affect their entitlement of Statutory Neonatal Care Pay:

Check if they have documentary evidence agreeing to the amount of Statutory Neonatal Care Pay that should have been paid to them, based on their average weekly earnings.

Then use the amount that’s been agreed to work out their average weekly earnings for Statutory Neonatal Care Pay.

If there’s no documentary evidence, use their gross earnings to work out their average weekly earnings for Statutory Neonatal Care Pay.

The employee can get advice from the HMRC Statutory Payment Dispute Team.

PAYE Settlement Agreements

If your employee was not eligible for Statutory Neonatal Care Pay because their average weekly earnings were less than the lower earnings limit at the end of the relevant week, you must:

Add up any expenses or benefits included in the PAYE Settlement Agreement received in the relevant period.

Include the total amount of any expenses or benefits in their gross earnings.

Then use their gross earnings to work out their average weekly earnings in the relevant period.

Salary sacrifice

If your employee has a salary sacrifice arrangement with you, use the actual amount of gross earnings paid to them during the relevant period to work out their average weekly earnings.

Statutory Neonatal Care Pay cannot be sacrificed and must be paid in full.

Find out more about salary sacrifice for employers.

Non-cash benefit

You may pay some of your employee’s earnings with a non-cash benefit, such as board and lodgings, goods or services.

The monetary value of the benefit given to your employee during the Statutory Neonatal Care Pay period cannot be deducted from their pay entitlement.

You must pay any Statutory Neonatal Care Pay in full.

Multiple births from the same pregnancy

Your employee will only be entitled to Statutory Neonatal Care Leave and Pay (if they’re eligible) for a maximum of 12 weeks, even if more than one baby needs neonatal care:

at the same time

at separate times

If more than one baby needs neonatal care at the same time, your employee can build up (‘accrue’) their entitlement of Statutory Neonatal Care Leave and Pay for one baby only.

If the babies need neonatal care at separate times, your employee can build up their entitlement of Statutory Neonatal Care Leave and Pay for each of the babies, as long as they each receive at least 7 full continuous days of neonatal care.

Your employee will have up to 68 weeks from the birth of the babies, or from the birth of the first baby (if the babies have different birth dates) to use up their entitlement.

Parental orders and surrogacy arrangements

If your employee is the intended parent in a surrogacy arrangement, they should apply for a parental order to become the baby’s legal parent within 6 months of the baby’s birth.

If they do not apply for a parental order, or it’s not approved, they’re entitled to Statutory Neonatal Care Pay if:

the baby starts to receive neonatal care within 28 days of being born, and they receive at least 7 full continuous days of neonatal care

they’ve already built up (‘accrued’) their entitlement of Statutory Neonatal Care Pay

They must take their entitlement within 68 weeks of the baby’s birth date.

Find out about surrogacy and the legal rights of parents.

Adoption disruption

If your employee is the adopting parent, and the adoption is disrupted, they’re entitled to Statutory Neonatal Care Pay if:

the baby starts to receive neonatal care within 28 days of being born, and they received at least 7 full continuous days of neonatal care

they’ve already built up (‘accrued’) their entitlement of Statutory Neonatal Care Pay

They must take their entitlement within 68 weeks of the baby’s birth date.

An adoption can be disrupted if, for example, the baby is returned to local authority care or adopted from overseas, but stops living with the adopting parent.

If the baby dies

Your employee is entitled to Statutory Neonatal Care Pay if:

the baby starts to receive neonatal care within 28 days of being born, and they received 7 full continuous days of neonatal care

they’ve already built up (‘accrued’) their entitlement of Statutory Neonatal Care Pay

They must take their entitlement within 68 weeks of the baby’s birth date.

They may also be eligible for Statutory Parental Bereavement Pay and Leave.

Employee is not returning to work

If your employee tells you that they’re not returning to work after they’ve taken their Statutory Neonatal Care Pay, you must carry on paying them their entitlement of Statutory Neonatal Care Pay.

You cannot ask them to pay any of it back.

Employee leaves before Statutory Neonatal Care Pay is taken
